client: I've been having this really uncomfortable thing happen whenever I walk into this café near my apartment. It's the place where my ex and I used to meet all the time, and the moment I step inside, my heart just starts racing and I feel completely overwhelmed, like I need to get out immediately. I keep avoiding it now, but honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how my body reacts in there.
therapist: What you're describing makes a lot of sense — that café has become deeply tied to memories of your ex, so your body is essentially sounding an alarm the moment you walk in, even before your thoughts catch up. I notice there's a quiet heaviness in how you're sharing this, like you're carrying some doubt about whether anything can really shift that physical reaction, which is completely understandable. The good news is that avoidance, while it feels protective right now, actually keeps that alarm system active — and there are gentle, gradual ways we can work together to help your mind and body learn that the café itself isn't the source of the pain.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying about avoidance keeping the alarm going, and part of me gets that logically. But honestly, when I think about actually going back in there, even just standing near the door, my stomach just drops and I can't imagine my body ever not reacting that way. It feels like the reaction is just... baked in at this point, like it's become part of who I am now.
therapist: The way you're speaking carries a real weight to it — there's something that sounds almost resigned, like a part of you has quietly accepted this reaction as permanent, even as you're still trying to reason your way through it. That belief — that this is just "who you are now" — is actually worth gently examining, because our nervous systems are remarkably adaptable, and what got learned through painful experience can also be gradually unlearned. It doesn't mean forcing yourself back in before you're ready, but rather that the story of "this is baked in forever" is a thought we can test, not a fact we have to accept.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I can see how it might be a thought rather than a fact, but testing it feels really daunting because what if I go back in and have a full panic attack in front of everyone? Like, the embarrassment on top of the anxiety just makes the whole idea feel even more impossible. It's not just the memory of my ex anymore, it's also this fear of losing control publicly that's kind of layered on top now.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, like the words are tumbling out under some pressure — really reflects how layered this has become, and it makes sense that what started as one fear has quietly grown into two. That second layer, the fear of being seen losing control, is actually very common and has a name in CBT — it's sometimes called "fear of fear," where the anxiety about having anxiety becomes its own obstacle. What's worth noticing is that your mind is jumping to a very specific, worst-case story about what *would* happen, and we could gently start to examine the evidence for that story before you ever have to set foot near that door.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Okay, "fear of fear" actually does kind of click for me, like I can recognize that pattern in myself. But when you say examining the evidence, I'm not totally sure what that looks like in practice, because in the moment it doesn't feel like a story, it feels completely real and certain. How do you actually examine something when your whole body is convinced it's true?
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of urgency — tells me this question feels really important to you, like you're genuinely reaching for something practical rather than just pushing back, and that's a really meaningful shift. You're absolutely right that in the middle of a panic, you can't just think your way out — so examining the evidence actually happens *before* the moment, when you're calmer, by asking questions like "how many times have I predicted I'd fully lose control in public, and how many times did that actually happen?" What we're doing is building a kind of mental toolkit ahead of time, so that when your body sounds the alarm, there's a small, practiced voice that can say "I've been here before and survived it."
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question actually stops me a bit, because when I think about it honestly, I haven't actually fully lost control in public before, even when I've felt completely certain I was about to. But I worry that this time feels different, like my brain is already telling me the café is the exception, the one place where it really would happen. How do I stop myself from just dismissing the evidence because my anxiety keeps insisting this situation is uniquely dangerous?
therapist: The tension in your voice — high and quick, like you're working hard to hold something together even as you're making a really honest breakthrough — tells me this realization is both meaningful and a little unsettling for you. What you've just done is actually the most important step: you caught your anxiety using a very specific trick called "special exception thinking," where it concedes the general evidence but insists *this* case is different — and simply being able to name that pattern in the moment weakens its grip. So next time your mind says "but the café is different," you can respond with "there it is again, that's the exception trick," and treat it as a signal that your anxiety is working hard, not as proof that the danger is real.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I actually kind of like the idea of calling it out like that, giving it a name in the moment, because it makes it feel less like this massive overwhelming force and more like a trick I can catch. But I'm a little skeptical about whether I'll actually remember to do that when I'm standing outside the café and my heart is already pounding, because in those moments my mind goes pretty blank. Is there a way to make that feel more automatic, or does it just take a lot of practice before it actually kicks in?
therapist: There's something genuinely energized in how you're speaking right now — fast, bright, like a part of you is actually getting excited about having a tool even while another part is still hedging, and that mix makes a lot of sense. The good news is that "automatic" is exactly what we're building toward, and the way to get there is through rehearsal in calm moments — actually picturing yourself outside that café, heart pounding, and mentally practicing saying "there's the exception trick," so your brain has already walked that path before the real moment arrives. It does take repetition, but you've already done the hardest part today, which is seeing the trick clearly enough to name it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: So the homework is basically just sitting somewhere safe and imagining the scenario in my head, like a mental rehearsal? I think I can try that, but I'm a little worried that even just picturing it might set off the anxiety, like my brain won't really distinguish between imagining it and actually being there. What if the rehearsal itself just becomes another thing I start avoiding?
therapist: Your voice is soft but moving quickly, like you're thinking this through carefully even as a quiet worry creeps in — and the concern you're raising is actually really astute, because you're right that your brain doesn't perfectly distinguish imagination from reality, but here's the reframe: that's precisely *why* the rehearsal works. We'd start very gently, maybe just imagining standing on the street outside, and if anxiety does show up during the rehearsal, that's not a failure — it's actually a perfect low-stakes opportunity to practice catching the exception trick in a safe space. The goal isn't to rehearse without any anxiety, it's to rehearse *responding to* the anxiety, so that avoiding the rehearsal itself becomes something you can recognize and name, just like we did today with the café.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That reframe actually helps, that the anxiety showing up during the rehearsal isn't me failing but is actually the point of it. I think I can try starting really small, just the street outside, and see what happens. I guess my only lingering worry is that I'll do the rehearsal a few times and still feel like I'm nowhere near ready to actually go in, and then I'll feel like I've been doing all this work for nothing.
therapist: There's something in your voice — high and quick, like you're genuinely engaged but also bracing slightly for disappointment — that tells me this worry about "work for nothing" is important to name, because it's actually another version of the all-or-nothing thinking your anxiety loves to use. Progress in this kind of work rarely looks like a straight line toward walking through that door — it looks like noticing the exception trick faster, or feeling the anxiety for thirty seconds instead of sixty, or choosing to do the rehearsal even when you didn't want to, and all of that counts. So rather than measuring success by whether you feel "ready," we could agree that showing up to the rehearsal at all, even when it's uncomfortable, *is* the work — and that's something you've already shown today you're capable of doing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Reframing it as smaller signs of progress actually makes it feel less like this impossible mountain I have to climb all at once. I think part of me has been so fixated on the end goal of walking back into that café that I've been dismissing everything in between as not really counting. It's a little uncomfortable to admit that, because it means I've kind of been setting myself up to feel like a failure before I even start.
therapist: There's something that sounds both relieved and a little raw in how you're saying this — like the words are coming out fast and bright, but underneath them is something tender, because recognizing a pattern we've been using against ourselves takes real courage. What you've just named — that the goalposts were set so far away that nothing in between could ever feel like enough — is actually one of the most important insights you can have, and it didn't come from me, it came from you looking honestly at your own thinking. That's not a small thing, and I'd gently invite you to let that count too.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: It's strange to hear you say it came from me, because I think I'm so used to feeling like I don't really have good insight into my own patterns that I almost want to dismiss it. But I'm trying to just sit with that for a second instead of immediately brushing it off, which is harder than it sounds. I think letting things count, even small things, might actually be the part I struggle with most.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — softly, carefully, like you're handling something fragile — really matches what you're describing, this quiet effort to just *stay* with something instead of deflecting it away. And what you're doing in this moment, choosing to sit with the discomfort of being seen as capable rather than immediately dismissing it, is itself a perfect example of letting something small count. The fact that it feels hard is actually the point — this might be the most important pattern we've uncovered today, and it started with you noticing it yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
